newsitem.title: ITALY: Food summit left guessing on Castro.
newsitem.headline: Food summit left guessing on Castro.

text.p: Cuban President Fidel Castro was given a prominent role at the U.N. sponsored World Food Summit when it opened on Wednesday but participants were left guessing whether he would attend or not.

Castro was named as one of six vice-chairmen for the five-day summit but his name does not figure on the official list of participants released by the hosts, the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), nor was he present.
According to the list, described as provisional, the Cuban delegation is headed by Food Industry Minister Alejandro Roca Iglesias.
Castro's movements traditionally are not released in advance, but his expected attendance at the summit is probably among the worst kept secrets in Rome.

Diplomatic sources say the veteran communist is expected to arrive in the early hours of Friday and should meet Italian leaders during his stay. An historic meeting with Pope John Paul is also possible.

Wednesday's official notification that he was among the summit's vice-chairmen was a further piece in the puzzle and should mean he will represent Latin America at a closing news conference on Sunday.
The summit, the world's first on hunger, is reserved for heads of state and government from Friday afternoon.
FAO director general Jacques Diouf has repeatedly said some 100 world leaders would attend although the FAO list of participants, excluding Castro, set the number at 83.
Almost half -- 41 -- are from Africa, the continent worst hit by hunger and malnutrition.
Two of the countries that are facing severe food problems are not attending. Liberia does not appear to have sent anyone while Somalia has not been invited, according to the list.

Libya has sent its Agriculture Minister Ali Ben Romdhan, who ended intense speculation in Italy over the past week that leader Muammar Gaddafi might use the summit to make a rare and stunning visit to the West.
"He is busy inside the country," the minister told Reuters, saying Gaddafi's non-participation had nothing to do with U.N. sanctions that include a ban on flights to and from Libya.
Most of the leaders of the world's richest nations, the Group of Seven industrialised countries, are also staying away.
Italy has sent Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who was named chairman of the summit, and France Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
Britain, Canada, Germany, Japan, and the United States are represented at ministerial level.
